title: Requirements
summary: Split functional needs from scale and drop features that do not change the design.

parts.rule: Separate functional requirements—user-visible operations—from quality constraints such as scale, latency, durability, availability, consistency, security, and cost. Rank the must-haves, attach numbers where they affect design, and explicitly park optional features after confirming that choice. Reopen scope when the interviewer changes a requirement.
parts.why: A system cannot optimize every property at once. A 5 GB upload, a 200 ms folder listing, and immediate conflict visibility imply different paths and tradeoffs. A short ranked list prevents the design from solving an imagined product while also giving each later component a requirement it can be traced back to.
parts.example: For a file-sync service, define four functional operations: upload or replace a file, download a file, list a folder, and create a revocable share link. Clarify that desktop and mobile clients are in scope but collaborative document editing is not. Add measurable constraints: files may be as large as 5 GB; a successful upload must survive a single storage-node failure; a typical folder list should finish below 200 ms at p95; two devices editing the same version must receive an explicit conflict instead of silently overwriting; and links may be revoked within 1 minute. Assume 10 million daily active users before doing traffic estimates. Park full-text search, OCR, and rich in-browser editing. These choices already shape the later design: large uploads suggest multipart transfer directly to object storage, folder listing needs metadata indexed by parent folder, and conflict visibility needs versions or conditional writes. Search would require an asynchronous content index, so add it only if the interviewer brings it back into scope. Notice that “fast,” “durable,” and “large scale” are not yet requirements; 200 ms, one-node failure, and 10 million users are concrete enough to evaluate.
parts.use: Write and confirm requirements before choosing components. Keep functional and quality lists visible, label assumptions, and ask which tradeoff matters when goals conflict. During the interview, challenge every new box to point to a requirement or a measured bottleneck.
parts.refuse: Do not treat “web scale” or “highly available” as usable constraints without numbers or failure scope. Avoid silently adding multi-region operation, analytics, search, and admin products to an MVP. Keep latency and durability targets out of the feature list, and do not continue with an assumption after the interviewer has changed it.

body:
Rule. Separate functional requirements—user-visible operations—from quality constraints such as scale, latency, durability, availability, consistency, security, and cost. Rank the must-haves, attach numbers where they affect design, and explicitly park optional features after confirming that choice. Reopen scope when the interviewer changes a requirement.

Why it matters. A system cannot optimize every property at once. A 5 GB upload, a 200 ms folder listing, and immediate conflict visibility imply different paths and tradeoffs. A short ranked list prevents the design from solving an imagined product while also giving each later component a requirement it can be traced back to.

Worked example. For a file-sync service, define four functional operations: upload or replace a file, download a file, list a folder, and create a revocable share link. Clarify that desktop and mobile clients are in scope but collaborative document editing is not. Add measurable constraints: files may be as large as 5 GB; a successful upload must survive a single storage-node failure; a typical folder list should finish below 200 ms at p95; two devices editing the same version must receive an explicit conflict instead of silently overwriting; and links may be revoked within 1 minute. Assume 10 million daily active users before doing traffic estimates. Park full-text search, OCR, and rich in-browser editing. These choices already shape the later design: large uploads suggest multipart transfer directly to object storage, folder listing needs metadata indexed by parent folder, and conflict visibility needs versions or conditional writes. Search would require an asynchronous content index, so add it only if the interviewer brings it back into scope. Notice that “fast,” “durable,” and “large scale” are not yet requirements; 200 ms, one-node failure, and 10 million users are concrete enough to evaluate.

[[diagram:split]]

When to use. Write and confirm requirements before choosing components. Keep functional and quality lists visible, label assumptions, and ask which tradeoff matters when goals conflict. During the interview, challenge every new box to point to a requirement or a measured bottleneck.

When to refuse. Do not treat “web scale” or “highly available” as usable constraints without numbers or failure scope. Avoid silently adding multi-region operation, analytics, search, and admin products to an MVP. Keep latency and durability targets out of the feature list, and do not continue with an assumption after the interviewer has changed it.
